title: Modelling commissioned by the Australian Conservation Foundation found powering data centres with small modular reactors would cost billions of dollars a year more than solar with storage
oneLiner: The 'Phantom Energy' report put the gap at between $6 billion and $11 billion a year.
body: The report compared the cost of meeting projected data-centre demand with small modular reactors against large-scale solar and storage, and found the nuclear option several billion dollars a year dearer. It also noted that no commercial reactor has yet been built with the modular factory methods meant to bring costs down.
contextBackground: This is the main factual reply to the data-centre argument. It was commissioned by an advocacy group opposed to nuclear, which is why it is rated moderate rather than strong; its inputs have not been independently audited.
contextDisagreement: Supporters of nuclear say the comparison assumes solar can meet a constant load and ignores the land and transmission costs of doing so; opponents say the gap is too large for those adjustments to close.

evidenceItems.citation: Canberra Times (AAP), 'Artificial intelligence, nuclear power a costly combo', 2026 — reporting the ACF-commissioned Phantom Energy analysis

otherClaim.title: AI data centres need large amounts of firm power that nuclear could supply

claimItself.title: AI data centres need large amounts of firm power that nuclear could supply
claimItself.oneLiner: The newest argument for repeal: a customer that wants constant, emissions-free electricity and can pay for it.
claimItself.body: Australia has more than 160 operating data centres and over 200 more proposed. The Coalition argues that lifting the ban would let private operators contract for nuclear power for these loads, without any public money, and that a legislated prohibition deters that investment before it is even assessed.
